A Li Dongyuan formula. A large dose of Huangqi strongly tonifies spleen and lung qi to support the source of blood production ("tangible blood is born from intangible qi"), paired with Danggui to nourish blood and harmonize the nutritive level. Original ratio Huangqi : Danggui = 5:1 (30g : 6g).

From Yixue Qiyuan: ginseng tonifies qi, Maidong nourishes yin and clears heat, Wuweizi preserves yin and stops sweating; one tonifies, one moistens, one astringes, together augmenting qi and generating fluids. Using American Ginseng gives a gentler, cooler tonic suited to summer damage of both qi and yin.

The foundational qi tonic from Taiping Huimin Hejiju Fang. Ginseng is the chief, tonifying original qi; Baizhu is the deputy, strengthening the spleen and drying dampness; Fuling is the assistant, draining dampness; Gancao is the envoy, harmonizing the middle.

The foundational blood-tonifying and blood-regulating formula. Shudi and Baishao are "blood herbs within the blood"; Danggui and Chuanxiong are "qi herbs within the blood", so it tonifies without causing stagnation.
Jade Windscreen Powder (Yu Ping Feng San), missing Fangfeng

Huangqi augments qi and consolidates the exterior, Baizhu strengthens the spleen; these form the core of Yu Ping Feng San. The original formula also includes Fangfeng (Saposhnikovia) to disperse wind.
Goji nourishes the kidney and liver (water), Chrysanthemum clears the liver and brightens the eyes (wood), embodying "nourishing water to moisten wood"; this is the core pair of Qi Ju Di Huang Wan.
The chief herbs of Sang Ju Yin: disperse wind-heat, clear the lung and brighten the eyes; commonly used for early-stage wind-heat cough.
Combines clearing heat and resolving toxicity with dispersing wind and brightening the eyes; suited to wind-heat with internal heat, sore throat and red eyes.

Fresh Ginger (acrid, warm) moves the defensive level; Jujube (sweet, warm) tonifies the nutritive level. Together they harmonize the nutritive and defensive qi, harmonize the stomach and stop vomiting; commonly used in Gui Zhi Tang and other formulas.
From Shang Han Lun: diffuses the lung and soothes the throat, expels phlegm and pus; commonly used for sore throat.

Suanzaoren Tang from Jingui Yaolue without Zhimu: nourishes blood and calms the spirit, clears heat and relieves irritability; indicated for "deficiency taxation with deficiency irritability and inability to sleep".
Two Aged Herbs Decoction (Er Chen Tang, variant)
Er Chen Tang lacking Banxia (Pinellia): regulates qi, dries dampness and resolves phlegm.
Sharen awakens the spleen and moves qi, countering the cloying, stomach-hindering nature of Shudihuang; an old method is "Shudi mixed with Sharen".
Chenpi regulates qi and strengthens the spleen so that tonification does not cause congestion.
Promotes digestion and dissolves accumulation, moves qi and harmonizes the stomach; commonly used for post-meal food stagnation.
Soothes the liver and relieves constraint, regulates qi and harmonizes the stomach; suited to emotional constraint with stomach bloating.
Clears the lung, soothes the throat and restores the voice; can be taken short-term as a tea for voice overuse.
Tonifies the heart and spleen, nourishes blood and calms the spirit.
Clears the liver and brightens the eyes, and also moistens the intestines to unblock the bowels.
Combines generating fluids and unblocking the collaterals with invigorating blood and resolving stasis; commonly used in modern cardio-cerebrovascular wellness approaches (follow medical advice).
Lily Bulb with Sour Jujube Seed
Clears the heart and moistens the lung, nourishes the liver and calms the spirit; suited to deficiency irritability and insomnia.
From Zhengti Leiyao: Four Gentlemen Decoction combined with Four Substances Decoction, tonifying both qi and blood.

The "light acrid-cool formula" of Wenbing Tiaobian: disperses wind and clears heat, diffuses the lung and stops cough. Original doses are very light (Sangye 7.5g, Juhua 3g), reflecting "treat the upper burner like a feather; only lightness can lift".
From Jingui Yaolue, indicated for "visceral agitation in women, with a tendency to sorrow and weeping": nourishes the heart and calms the spirit, harmonizes the middle and relaxes urgency.
Jiegeng Tang with Xuanshen and Maidong added: nourishes yin, clears heat and soothes the throat; suited to yin-deficient dry throat and voice overuse.
A famous Fujian-Taiwan medicinal cuisine formula: strengthens the spleen and dispels dampness, consolidates the kidney and stops diarrhea; neutral in nature and suitable for regular use.
Shanzha excels at digesting meat, Maiya at flour and starches, Shenqu at grain accumulation; together they dissolve all kinds of food stagnation.

Derived from a Qing imperial kitchen recipe: Wumei generates fluids and astringes the lung, Shanzha promotes digestion; sour and sweet combine to transform into yin. A traditional drink for relieving summer-heat and thirst.
A classic Lingnan herbal tea: clears the liver and brightens the eyes, disperses wind and heat.
A folk blood-nourishing formula, "using red to nourish red": tonifies blood and nourishes the heart, strengthens the spleen and promotes urination.
Promotes urination, drains dampness and strengthens the spleen; commonly used for heavy dampness. Both are draining, so not suitable for prolonged use in those with fluid deficiency.
Acrid-warm exterior release, moves qi and harmonizes the stomach; commonly used for early wind-cold common cold with stomach discomfort.

From Hanshi Yitong: Huanglian clears heart fire, Rougui warms kidney yang and guides fire back to its source; using cold and hot together to restore heart-kidney communication. Original ratio Huanglian : Rougui approx. 10:1.
Coptis and Ejiao Decoction (Huanglian Ejiao Tang)

From Shang Han Lun (the original also contains egg yolk): Huanglian and Huangqin clear heart fire, Ejiao and Baishao nourish yin and blood; indicated for "vexation in the heart with inability to lie down (sleep)".
From Yifang Jijie: Nvzhenzi is harvested at the winter solstice and Mohanlian at the summer solstice, hence the name. Tonifies the liver and kidney, nourishes yin and stops bleeding; mild in nature.
Baimaogen cools blood and promotes urination, Lugen clears heat and generates fluids; the two roots together clear heat without damaging fluids.
The composition of Da Chuanxiong Wan: Chuanxiong invigorates blood, dispels wind and relieves pain, Tianma calms the liver and extinguishes wind; treats head-wind and dizziness.
Qi-regulating herbs counter the cloying, stomach-hindering nature of Ejiao.
The German household Fenchel-Anis-Kümmel tea: three carrot-family seeds in equal parts, carminative and antispasmodic, used for bloating in adults and children. Crush before use.
The core of the German pharmacopoeia “sweat tea” (Species diaphoreticae): drink hot, keep warm and sweat, at the onset of a cold.
The cold tea of British herbal tradition, in equal parts: promotes sweating, disperses wind and opens the nose.
A fixed combination approved by Commission E: valerian and hops act together as a sedative, often with lemon balm. Do not drive afterwards.
The most common European stomach pairing: chamomile relieves spasm and inflammation, peppermint is carminative and settles nausea.
The classic German fruit tea Hagebutte-Hibiskus: tart, thirst-quenching and deep red.

"Sargassum, Euphorbia, Kansui and Genkwa all oppose Licorice": Licorice is incompatible with Sargassum; using them together may increase toxicity or cause adverse reactions, and they should not be combined in a wellness formula.
"Clove must not meet Curcuma": Clove is antagonized by Curcuma Tuber; traditionally they are not used together.
Ginseng is inhibited by Radish Seed: Laifuzi directs qi downward and dissolves accumulation, weakening the qi-tonifying power of Ginseng.
When ginseng-type herbs are used with Radish Seed, their qi-tonifying power is weakened by its qi-descending, digestive action.
Dangshen tonifies and Laifuzi disperses, so the tonifying effect is reduced; may be kept if intended deliberately to "tonify without causing stagnation".

All herbs mean dried, cut herbs bought from a pharmacy or a reliable supplier (some stir-fried, roasted or steamed); grams are dry weight. Apart from fresh ginger and scallion, none are fresh plants. Never forage wild plants yourself: many poisonous plants look like medicinal ones, such as gelsemium and honeysuckle, or pokeweed and ginseng.
